NCAA Performance Technologies
Recommendations
Comprehensive Action Plan for Baylor Athletics
Prepared by Coach Rash
Baylor University Department of Athletics
March 2026
WORKING DOCUMENT
For internal use. Subject to revision based on stakeholder input.
Table of Contents
Introduction
In March 2026, the NCAA Sport Science Institute published Performance Technologies Recommendations: Responsible Use in Collegiate Athletics, a consensus document developed from the May 2025 NCAA Summit on Performance Technologies. The document provides member schools with a framework for responsibly using performance technologies, organized around five core recommendations: Policy, Education, Data Management, Technology Selection, and Continuous Improvement.
This action plan translates those recommendations into a detailed, Baylor-specific implementation roadmap. Each section includes the NCAA language, what it means for our department, specific action items with assigned deliverables, and draft templates or sample language that the working group can adapt as we move forward.
Baylor Athletics does not currently have formal performance technology policies in place. This plan is designed to build the foundation from scratch, leveraging existing structures (annual compliance sessions, SAAC, campus IT, and legal resources) wherever possible.
How to Use This Document
Each recommendation section follows a consistent structure:
Blue callout box: The NCAA recommendation language, quoted directly.
Gold callout box: The specific NCAA strategy statement being addressed.
"What This Means for Baylor": Plain-language interpretation of how this applies to us.
Key Actions: Checkbox items for the working group to track.
Deliverable: The specific output expected from each action area.
Draft Templates: Sample language, forms, or frameworks ready for adaptation.
Recommendation 1: Policy
What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools establish a written plan that addresses the responsible use of performance technologies. Having a written plan can help establish common standards and procedures, increase transparency ,  and address school-specific needs and resources.
What This Means for Baylor
We need a formal, written policy document that serves as the governing framework for how Baylor Athletics uses performance technologies. This is not a one-time exercise. The NCAA expects it to be developed by a cross-functional team, reviewed regularly, and updated as technologies and needs evolve. Every other recommendation in this document (education, data management, purchasing, and feedback) ties back to this written plan.
Strategy 1.1: Assemble a Multidisciplinary Working Group
NCAA Strategy:  Engage a multidisciplinary team in developing, routinely reviewing ,  and revising a written plan, leveraging existing campus resources and systems. Key roles on that team may include, but are not limited to, student-athletes, sports medicine staff, coaches, athletics administration, legal affairs ,  and information technology.
Key Actions:
Identify a chair/lead for the working group. This person should have the organizational authority to coordinate across departments and the bandwidth to drive the process forward. Recommended candidates: Associate AD for Student-Athlete Services, Director of Sports Medicine, or a senior administrator with cross-departmental oversight.
Recruit representatives from each required area. The NCAA specifically names the following roles. Each representative should have decision-making authority or direct access to decision-makers in their area:
Student-Athletes: Minimum two representatives, ideally from different sports and genders. SAAC members or sport captains are strong candidates. Their voice is not advisory; it is essential.
Sports Medicine/Athletic Training: Head athletic trainer or designee. This person will be critical for data management (Rec 3) and ensuring the independent medical authority is protected.
Strength and Conditioning: Director of S&C or senior staff member. S&C is typically the primary operator of wearable technologies and force plates.
Coaching: Minimum two sport representatives from different sports. Coaches are end-users of performance data and need a seat at the table.
Athletics Administration: Associate AD or senior administrator who can approve policy and allocate resources.
Legal Affairs/Compliance: University legal counsel or athletics compliance officer. Essential for data privacy, consent, and regulatory considerations.
Information Technology: Campus IT or athletics IT representative. Responsible for data security, storage, vendor integration, and breach response.
Define the group charter. The working group should have a clear written charter that includes:
Mission: Develop, maintain, and oversee Baylor Athletics' written plan for the responsible use of performance technologies.
Scope: All performance technologies used across Baylor Athletics, including devices, software, apps, and surveys that collect biometric or performance data.
Responsibilities: Draft and maintain the written plan, review and approve new technology purchases, oversee education programs, collect and act on feedback, and ensure compliance with applicable laws.
Meeting cadence: Monthly during initial development (March through June 2026), then quarterly once the plan is established.
Decision-making: Consensus-based where possible; chair breaks ties. Legal has veto authority on compliance matters.
Set the initial meeting schedule. Book monthly meetings through June 2026. The first meeting should focus on reviewing this document and the NCAA source material, and on assigning ownership of plan sections.
Deliverable:
Working Group Charter Document (1-2 pages) documenting mission, membership, roles, meeting cadence, and decision-making process.
Draft Template: Working Group Charter
Section | Content
Purpose | Establish and maintain Baylor Athletics' written plan for the responsible use of performance technologies in alignment with NCAA Sport Science Institute recommendations.
Membership | Chair: [TBD] Student-Athletes: [Names, Sports] Sports Medicine: [Name, Title] S&C: [Name, Title] Coaching: [Name, Sport] and [Name, Sport] Administration: [Name, Title] Legal/Compliance: [Name, Title] IT: [Name, Title]
Meeting Cadence | Monthly (March-June 2026), Quarterly (July 2026 onward)
Responsibilities | 1. Develop written plan 2. Review/approve new technology purchases 3. Oversee education programs 4. Collect and act on feedback 5. Ensure legal/regulatory compliance
Decision Process | Consensus-based; Chair breaks ties. Legal holds veto on compliance matters.
Reporting | Chair reports to [AD/Senior Administrator] after each meeting.
Review | Charter reviewed annually at the first meeting of each academic year.
Strategy 1.2: Draft the Written Plan
NCAA Strategy:  Address school-specific considerations, including how relevant groups will be educated, how data will be managed, how decisions will be made about selecting and implementing new technologies and how continuous improvement will be approached.
The written plan is the central deliverable. It should be a single, comprehensive document (or a policy manual with clearly organized sections) that anyone in the department can reference. Below is the recommended structure and the content each section should address.
Key Actions:
Create a policy document organized around the following sections:
Plan Section | Content to Address | Owner
1. Purpose & Scope | Why the plan exists, what it covers, which technologies and personnel fall under it | Chair
2. Definitions | Performance technology, biometric data, performance data, informed consent, data steward, etc. | Chair + Legal
3. Roles & Responsibilities | Who does what : Working Group, coaches, S&C, sports medicine, IT, student-athletes, administration | Chair
4. Student-Athlete Rights | Informed consent process, right to decline, data access rights, grievance process | Legal
5. Data Governance | Data ownership, storage, access controls, retention, transfer protocol, breach response (see Rec 3) | IT + Legal
6. Technology Evaluation | Criteria and process for vetting new technologies before purchase (see Rec 4) | S&C + Sports Med
7. Education Requirements | Who gets trained, how often, on what topics, and how completion is tracked (see Rec 2) | Chair
8. Continuous Improvement | Feedback mechanisms, annual review process, plan revision protocol (see Rec 5) | Chair
9. Compliance | Applicable laws (FERPA, state privacy, biometric), NCAA guidance references, institutional policies | Legal + Compliance
10. Appendices | Consent form template, tech evaluation checklist, education curriculum outlines, feedback survey | Various
Route the draft through legal affairs and compliance for review. Legal should review for: applicable privacy laws (FERPA, Texas data privacy, any biometric privacy considerations), adequacy of informed consent language, data breach notification obligations, and alignment with university-wide policies.
Establish version control. Use a naming convention (e.g., BaylorAthletics_PerfTech_Policy_v1.0_2026-06) and maintain a revision log on the first page of the document. Store the master copy in a central location accessible to all working group members.
Set an annual review date. The plan should be reviewed at least annually. Recommend tying the review to the start of each academic year (August/September) so updates can be communicated during preseason meetings.
Deliverable:
Baylor Athletics Performance Technology Policy (estimated 15-25 pages with appendices). Target completion: June 2026.
Milestone | Description | Target Date
Working Group Formed | Chair identified, members recruited, charter signed | March 2026
First Meeting | Review  the  NCAA document, assign plan sections to owners | Early April 2026
Section Drafts Due | Each owner submits their section draft to the chair | Late April 2026
Full Draft Assembled | Chair compiles all sections into  a  unified document | Early May 2026
Legal/Compliance Review | Legal reviews full draft, provides redlines | Mid-May 2026
Working Group Final Review | Group reviews legal feedback, makes final edits | Late May 2026
Plan Approved | Chair and AD sign off; plan distributed to department | June 2026
First Annual Review | Working group reviews and updates the plan | August/September 2026
Recommendation 2: Education
What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools routinely provide education about the responsible use of performance technologies to those involved with their use. Education is foundational for informed consent, and it aids in ensuring schools use performance technologies in a way that maximizes benefits and minimizes harm to student-athletes.
What This Means for Baylor
Everyone who touches performance technology needs training, and that training needs to happen at least once a year. The good news: Baylor already has annual compliance and onboarding sessions. We can build performance technology modules into those existing structures rather than creating an entirely new training apparatus. The key is tailoring the content to different audiences, because a student-athlete and a compliance officer need very different information.
Strategy 2.1: Provide Annual Education to All Involved
NCAA Strategy:  At least once annually, provide education to those involved in selecting, using or accessing data from performance technologies.
Key Actions:
Map every person/role that interacts with performance technology. Create a comprehensive list of who selects, operates, interprets, accesses, or makes decisions based on performance technology data. This becomes your required-training roster.
Integrate performance technology training into existing annual sessions:
Staff annual compliance meeting: Add a 30-45 minute performance technology module covering policy overview, data handling responsibilities, and any updates from the previous year.
New student-athlete orientation: Add a 20-30 minute segment on performance technology rights, informed consent, what data is collected, and how to raise concerns.
Returning student-athlete preseason meeting: Add a brief (10-15 minute) refresher covering any new technologies introduced, policy changes, or updated consent requirements.
New hire onboarding: Include performance technology policy review for any new coaches, S&C staff, athletic trainers, or administrators.
Create an attendance tracking system. Use sign-in sheets or digital tracking (LMS if available) to document who completed training and when. This is your compliance record if questions arise.
Store all training materials centrally. Maintain a shared folder (e.g., on the athletics shared drive or LMS) with all slide decks, handouts, and reference materials so staff can review them at any time.
Deliverable:
An annual education calendar that maps each audience to their training session, timing, and delivery method.
Draft Template: Annual Education Calendar
Audience | Session | Timing | Duration | Delivery | Tracked?
All Staff | Annual Compliance Meeting | August (preseason) | 30-45 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
New Student-Athletes | Orientation | August/January | 20-30 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
Returning SAs | Preseason Meeting | August | 10-15 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
New Hires | Onboarding | Within 30 days of hire | 30 min | 1-on-1 or small group | HR checklist
Working Group | Annual Review Meeting | September | 60-90 min | In-person | Meeting minutes
Strategy 2.2: Tailor Education by Audience
NCAA Strategy:  Educational needs are likely to vary among different groups and schools should consider tailoring education to meet each group's learning needs. Such groups may include, but are not limited to, student-athletes, coaches, strength and conditioning staff, sports medicine staff and administration.
A one-size-fits-all presentation will not work. Below is a detailed breakdown of what each audience needs to know, along with sample talking points and curriculum outlines.
Key Actions:
Develop a Student-Athlete Education Module covering:
What performance technologies are and why Baylor uses them.
Exactly what data is collected about them (types, frequency, devices).
Who can see their data and who cannot (access controls by role).
How their data is stored, how long it is kept, and what happens when they graduate or transfer.
Their right to informed consent: what they are agreeing to, that participation is voluntary, how to withdraw, and that declining will not affect their standing on the team.
Potential negative effects to watch for (data fixation, anxiety about metrics, body image concerns from body composition tracking) and who to talk to if they experience them.
How to raise concerns or file a complaint about how their data is being used.
Draft Template: Sample Student-Athlete Talking Points
Topic | Key Message
What We Collect | We use [GPS trackers/heart rate monitors/body comp tools/wellness surveys/etc.] to help us keep you healthy and help you perform your best. Here is specifically what each tool measures.
Who Sees It | Your data is shared only with [specific roles]. Coaches can see [specific data types]. They cannot see [restricted data types]. Sports medicine has access to health-related data to make medical decisions.
Your Rights | You have the right to know what is collected, ask questions, and decline participation without penalty. If you consent, you can withdraw at any time.
Data After You Leave | When you graduate, your data is [retained for X years/deleted within X days]. If you transfer, [transfer protocol summary].
If Something Feels Wrong | If you feel stressed about your data, if someone is using it in a way that feels inappropriate, or if you have any questions, talk to [contact person/title]. You can also raise concerns through [SAAC/anonymous reporting process].
Develop a Coaches Education Module covering:
Overview of available performance technologies and what data they produce.
What data coaches are permitted to access and what is restricted (e.g., medical data, mental health screening results).
Limitations of performance technology data: these are tools, not crystal balls. Data should supplement coaching judgment, not replace it.
Responsible communication about data with student-athletes (avoid using data punitively or publicly).
The boundary between coaching decisions and medical decisions: sports medicine retains independent, unchallengeable authority over medical management and return-to-play.
Departmental policies and the consequences of policy violations.
Develop modules for S&C Staff, Sports Medicine, and Administration. Each should be tailored to their specific responsibilities as outlined in the audience focus table below:
Audience | Primary Focus Areas | Estimated Length
Student-Athletes | Rights, consent, data use, mental health, how to raise concerns | 20-30 min
Coaches | Responsible use, data access boundaries, limitations, independent medical authority | 30 min
S&C Staff | Device operation, data collection protocols, quality control, escalation to sports medicine | 30-45 min
Sports Medicine | Data-informed clinical decisions, independent medical authority, privacy obligations, return-to-play | 30 min
Administration | Policy compliance, risk management, legal obligations, procurement oversight, data security | 30 min
IT | Data storage, encryption, access controls, vendor security review, breach response protocols | 30 min
Strategy 2.3: Address Required Topics
NCAA Strategy:  Address topics  such as:  limitations and potential harms of performance technologies; data privacy and security; student-athlete rights and protections (e.g., informed consent); departmental policies and procedures for responsible use.
The NCAA names four specific topic areas. All four should appear in every audience module, though the depth and emphasis will vary. Below is a more detailed breakdown of what each topic should cover.
Required Topic | What to Cover | Why It Matters
1. Limitations & Potential Harms | No technology is perfectly accurate. Results can be misleading if context is missing. Mental health risks include data fixation, anxiety, body image concerns. Over-reliance on data can undermine coaching instincts and athlete autonomy. | Prevents overconfidence in data and protects student-athlete well-being.
2. Data Privacy & Security | What data is collected, where it is stored, who can access it, how long it is retained, what happens in a breach, and what laws apply (FERPA, state privacy, etc.). | Legal obligation and trust-building with student-athletes.
3. Student-Athlete Rights | Informed consent process, voluntary participation, right to withdraw, right to access own data, right to know how data is used, grievance process. | Foundational to ethical use and NCAA expectations.
4. Departmental Policies | Overview of the written plan, roles and responsibilities, technology evaluation process, feedback mechanisms, consequences for policy violations. | Ensures  everyone operates under the same standards.
Deliverable:
Five audience-specific training modules (slide decks and/or handouts) covering all four required topics, tailored to each group. Target completion: June 2026 for initial versions; reviewed and updated annually.
Recommendation 3: Data Management
What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools establish who owns data from performance technologies, where and how data is stored, who has the authority to access data and how data is permitted to be used. Performance technologies have different use-case scenarios and produce different types of data, and the interpretation and communication of data may benefit from a multidisciplinary approach.
What This Means for Baylor
This is the most complex recommendation because it sits at the intersection of legal, IT, sports medicine, and coaching. We need clear, documented answers to four questions: Who owns the data? Where does it live? Who can see it? What can it be used for? We also need specific protocols for transfer student-athletes and for situations where data informs medical decisions.
Strategy 3.1: Define Who Interprets and Shares Data
NCAA Strategy:  Determine who can be involved in interpreting and sharing/communicating data from performance technologies, including considerations for the required competencies and oversight necessary to do so effectively and responsibly.
Key Actions:
Create a Data Touchpoint Map. For every performance technology currently in use (identified during the technology inventory), document: what data it produces, who collects it, who interprets it, who it is shared with, and where it is stored.
Draft Template: Data Touchpoint Map
Technology | Data Produced | Collected By | Interpreted By | Shared With | Stored Where
[e.g., GPS Tracker] | Distance, speed, acceleration, player load | S&C Staff | S&C / Sport Scientist | Coaches (summary), Sports Med (if injury-related) | [Vendor cloud / campus server]
[e.g., Heart Rate Monitor] | HR, HRV, recovery metrics | S&C Staff | S&C / Sports Med | Sports Med (clinical), Coaches (aggregate only) | [Vendor platform]
[e.g., Body Comp Tool] | Body fat %, lean mass, etc. | Sports Med / S&C | Sports Med | Restricted: Sports Med only unless SA consents to share | [Campus server]
[e.g., Wellness Survey] | Sleep, soreness, stress, mood | S&C / Sports Med | Sports Med / Sport Psych | Coaches (flagged concerns only, no raw scores) | [Survey platform]
[Add rows as needed] |  |  |  |  | 
Define competency requirements for data interpretation. Not everyone should be interpreting every type of data. Establish minimum qualifications:
Health-related data (HRV, wellness, body composition): Interpretation restricted to sports medicine staff, licensed athletic trainers, or individuals with documented sports science credentials.
Training load and performance data (GPS, force plates, velocity): Interpretation by certified S&C professionals or individuals with sports science competencies.
Aggregate/summary data (team averages, trends): May be shared with coaches and administration in summarized form, with context provided by the interpreting professional.
Establish data sharing rules. Create a clear matrix showing who can share what with whom:
Data Type | Sports Med | S&C | Coaches | Administration | Student-Athlete
Individual health/medical | Full access | Flagged concerns only | No access | No access | Full access (own data)
Individual training load | Full access | Full access | Summary with context | No access | Full access (own data)
Individual body comp | Full access | With SA consent | No access | No access | Full access (own data)
Wellness survey (raw) | Full access | Flagged concerns only | No access | No access | Full access (own data)
Team aggregates | Full access | Full access | Full access | Summary reports | Team-level only
Assign a Data Steward. Designate one person responsible for overseeing compliance with data policies, managing access requests, and serving as the point of contact for data-related questions. Recommended: someone in sports medicine or athletics administration with IT coordination.
Deliverable:
Data Touchpoint Map and Data Access Matrix documents. Target: April 2026 (draft), May 2026 (finalized with legal review).
Strategy 3.2: Clarify Data Ownership and Rights
NCAA Strategy:  Determine what rights, if any, the school has with respect to data  collection, data use , data access and ownership of the performance technology data, including considerations for transfer student-athletes.
Key Actions:
Conduct a vendor contract audit. For every technology platform in use, pull the contract/terms of service and identify:
Who owns the data: Baylor, the student-athlete, or the vendor?
Where data is stored: On-premise, vendor cloud, third-party servers? In what jurisdiction?
Data retention: How long does the vendor keep data? Can we request deletion?
Data portability: Can we export our data if we switch vendors? In what format?
Breach notification: What is the vendor obligated to do if there is a data breach?
Work with legal to establish Baylor's position on data ownership. The recommendation is that Baylor assert ownership of all performance technology data collected from its student-athletes, with the student-athlete retaining the right to access their own data.
Develop a Transfer Student-Athlete Data Protocol:
Outgoing transfers: Student-athlete may request a copy of their data. Baylor retains its copy for [defined retention period]. Data is not proactively sent to the new school without the student-athlete's written request.
Incoming transfers: Baylor does not request performance technology data from the previous school. If the student-athlete voluntarily provides data, it is reviewed by sports medicine before being incorporated into Baylor systems.
Data deletion: Student-athletes may request deletion of their data upon departure, subject to any legal retention requirements.
Build data rights into the informed consent form. The consent form (see template below) should clearly state: what data is collected, how it will be used, who will access it, how long it will be retained, what happens at graduation/transfer, and how to withdraw consent.
Draft Template: Draft Informed Consent Form (Key Sections)
Section | Sample Language
Purpose | Baylor Athletics uses performance technologies to support your health, safety, and athletic performance. This form explains what data we collect, how we use it, and your rights regarding that data.
Technologies Used | [List specific technologies used by the student-athlete's sport, e.g., "Catapult GPS units during practice and competition, InBody body composition scans, daily wellness surveys via [platform]."]
Data Collected | The following types of data may be collected: [list specific data types, e.g., heart rate, GPS movement data, body composition measurements, sleep quality, self-reported wellness scores].
How Data Is Used | Your data will be used to: monitor training load and recovery, support injury prevention, inform return-to-play decisions (by sports medicine staff), and evaluate the effectiveness of training programs.
Who Has Access | Your data will be accessible to: [list specific roles and what they can see, consistent with the Data Access Matrix]. Your individual data will not be shared with anyone outside these roles without your written permission.
Your Rights | Participation is voluntary. You may decline to participate or withdraw consent at any time without penalty or impact on your athletic scholarship, playing time, or standing on the team. You have the right to: view your own data, ask questions about how it is used, and request corrections or deletion (subject to legal retention requirements).
Data Retention | Your data will be retained for [X years] after your departure from Baylor Athletics. After this period, data will be securely deleted. You may request earlier deletion upon departure.
Transfer Protocol | If you transfer to another institution, your data will not be sent to the new school without your written request. You may request a copy of your data at any time.
Contact | If you have questions or concerns about your data, contact [Data Steward name, title, email, phone].
Signature | I have read and understand this consent form. I voluntarily agree to participate in performance technology data collection as described above.  Student-Athlete Signature: _____________ Date: _______ Printed Name: _______________
Deliverable:
Informed Consent Form Template (reviewed and approved by legal). Transfer Student-Athlete Data Protocol (1-2 pages). Vendor Contract Audit Summary (spreadsheet). Target: May 2026.
Strategy 3.3: Establish Permissible Uses of Data
NCAA Strategy:  Clarify the school's permissible uses of data from performance technologies. If data might be used to inform medical decision-making, sports medicine staff should be involved. Schools should refer to independent medical care best practices to ensure the unchallengeable, autonomous authority of primary athletics healthcare providers to determine medical management and return-to-play decisions.
Key Actions:
Create an Approved Uses / Prohibited Uses list:
Approved Uses | Prohibited Uses
Monitoring training load to prevent overtraining | Using data to punish or publicly shame a student-athlete
Supporting injury prevention through workload management | Sharing individual data with media, NIL partners, or agents without written SA consent
Informing  return-to-play decisions (sports medicine only) | Using body composition data to restrict access to meals or dining
Evaluating effectiveness of training programs | Making  scholarship  or roster decisions based solely on technology data
Identifying trends that may indicate injury risk | Allowing coaches to override sports medicine return-to-play decisions based on performance data
Supporting sport science research (with IRB approval and SA consent) | Selling or sharing data with third parties
Providing student-athletes with their own data upon request | Retaining data beyond the stated retention period without legal basis
Codify independent medical authority. Include explicit language in the written plan stating that sports medicine staff retain final, unchallengeable authority over all medical management and return-to-play decisions, regardless of what performance technology data may suggest. Coaches and administrators may not override medical judgment based on data. Reference the NCAA Independent Medical Care Best Practices.
Coordinate with IT on data security. Work with IT to ensure:
All performance technology data is stored on encrypted systems.
Access is controlled through role-based permissions (matching the Data Access Matrix).
Backup and disaster recovery procedures are in place.
A data breach response plan exists and is tested.
Deliverable:
Approved/Prohibited Uses Policy (included in the written plan). Independent Medical Authority Statement (included in the written plan). IT Data Security Checklist (coordinated with campus IT). Target: May 2026.
Recommendation 4: Selecting & Implementing New Technologies
What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools establish a structured process for making decisions about selecting and implementing new performance technologies. A structured process that considers how to use performance technologies in a way that maximizes benefits and minimizes harm is important to ensure student-athlete well-being is prioritized.
What This Means for Baylor
No more ad hoc purchasing. Every new technology, whether it is a wearable device, a software platform, a mobile app, or a survey tool, should go through a defined evaluation process before it is purchased and deployed. The NCAA wants this to be a group decision driven by evidence, not a single department acting on vendor marketing.
Strategy 4.1: Use Evidence-Based Evaluation Standards
NCAA Strategy:  Review technologies using existing, evidence-based standards and frameworks that evaluate their value, usability ,  and quality.
Key Actions:
Develop a Technology Evaluation Checklist that every proposed technology must complete before purchase approval. The checklist should be filled out by the requesting department and reviewed by the Working Group.
Draft Template: Technology Evaluation Checklist
Evaluation Criteria | Questions to Answer | Score (1-5)
1. Scientific Validity | Is there peer-reviewed research supporting the technology's claims? Has it been validated in collegiate or athletic populations? Are the vendor's claims backed by independent evidence? | [  ]
2. Accuracy | Does the device measure what it claims to measure? What is the margin of error? Has accuracy been tested across different conditions (e.g., different sports, environments)? | [  ]
3. Reliability | Does the device produce consistent results under the same conditions? What is the test-retest reliability? | [  ]
4. Data Security | Where is data stored? Is it encrypted? Who has access? What is the vendor's breach notification policy? Is the vendor compliant with relevant regulations? | [  ]
5. Data Portability | Can data be exported in standard formats? What happens to data if we discontinue the platform? | [  ]
6. Usability | How easy is it to use for staff and student-athletes? What training is required? Is the user interface intuitive? | [  ]
7. Integration | Does it integrate with our existing systems? Are there compatibility issues with other technologies we use? | [  ]
8. Cost-Benefit | What is the total cost (purchase, subscription, maintenance, training)? Does the expected value justify the expense? What is the expected ROI? | [  ]
9. Fit with Program Needs | Does this technology solve an actual problem we have? Or is it a solution looking for a problem? Is there a cheaper or simpler alternative? | [  ]
10. Student-Athlete Impact | Could this technology have unintended negative effects on student-athlete well-being? Does it require significant time or effort from student-athletes? | [  ]
Scoring: 1 = Does not meet criteria, 5 = Fully meets criteria. A technology should score at a minimum of 3 on every criterion and achieve an average of 3.5 or above to proceed. Any score of 1 on Data Security or Student-Athlete Impact is an automatic rejection.
Deliverable:
Technology Evaluation Checklist Template (1-page form + scoring rubric). Target: May 2026.
Strategy 4.2: Assess Quality Before Committing
NCAA Strategy:  Consider and assess the quality of performance technologies. Quality may include, but is not limited to, factors such as accuracy, reliability, validity ,  and function.
Key Actions:
Require a pilot/trial period before full purchase whenever possible. Negotiate with vendors for a 30–60-day trial with a single sport or team before committing to a department-wide purchase. During the pilot, collect structured user feedback.
Request validation data from vendors. Ask for independent (non-vendor-funded) research demonstrating accuracy and reliability. If no independent research exists, that is a red flag worth noting on the evaluation checklist.
Check with peer institutions. Before purchasing, reach out to at least two comparable programs (Big 12 or Power conference) to ask about their experience with the technology. Document the feedback.
Conduct a post-implementation review. 90 days after deploying a new technology, the requesting department should report back to the Working Group on: whether the technology is performing as expected, user satisfaction, any issues encountered, and whether it should continue.
Draft Template: Pilot Evaluation Report
Section | Content
Technology Name | [Name, vendor, version]
Pilot Duration | [Start date] to [End date]
Sport/Team | [Sport used during pilot]
Requesting Department | [S&C / Sports Med / Coaching / etc.]
Purpose | Why we are evaluating this technology and what problem it is intended to solve.
Evaluation Checklist Score | [Overall score from the Technology Evaluation Checklist]
Pilot Findings | Did the technology perform as claimed? Were there accuracy or reliability issues? How did staff and student-athletes respond?
User Feedback Summary | What did staff say? What did student-athletes say?
Issues Encountered | Any technical problems, data security concerns, integration challenges, or negative student-athlete feedback?
Recommendation | Approve for full purchase / Extend pilot / Do not purchase. Rationale:
Submitted By | [Name, Title, Date]
Strategy 4.3: Multidisciplinary Purchase Decisions
NCAA Strategy:  Decisions about selecting and implementing performance technologies should be made by a multidisciplinary group. Important roles to consider  include sports medicine staff and individuals with competencies in sports science, coaching staff, information technology, data security, administration,  and compliance.
Key Actions:
Route all new technology purchase requests through the Working Group. No performance technology should be purchased without Working Group review and approval. This includes free tools, trial conversions, and platforms offered through sponsorship deals.
Establish a standard purchase request process:
Step 1: Requesting department completes the Technology Evaluation Checklist.
Step 2: IT reviews the data security section and provides written clearance or flags concerns.
Step 3: Sports medicine reviews student-athlete health/safety implications.
Step 4: Legal/compliance reviews vendor contract terms, data ownership, and regulatory considerations.
Step 5: Working Group reviews full package and votes to approve, request a pilot, or deny.
Step 6: If approved, finance/administration handles procurement. If a pilot is requested, see the pilot process above.
Document every decision. Maintain a log of all technology requests, evaluation scores, decisions, and rationale. This creates an audit trail and supports future decision-making.
Deliverable:
Technology Purchase Request Process (flowchart + written procedure). Purchase Decision Log (spreadsheet). Target: May 2026.
Recommendation 5: Continuous Improvement
What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools routinely get feedback from those using performance technologies about how these technologies are being used and how they are working. This feedback can be used to inform  changes  to the school's written plan to reflect current needs, available resources and evolving technological developments.
What This Means for Baylor
The written plan is a living document. The NCAA expects us to actively monitor how technologies are being used, whether they are delivering value, and, most importantly, whether student-athletes are experiencing any negative effects. Student-athlete feedback is not a nice-to-have; the NCAA calls it "critical." We need structured mechanisms to collect, interpret, and act on feedback from all stakeholders.
Strategy 5.1: Multidisciplinary Feedback Collection
NCAA Strategy:  Engage a multidisciplinary group to plan, collect ,  and interpret feedback about performance technologies. When possible, this group should include individuals involved in establishing the school's written plan for responsible use.
Key Actions:
Task the Working Group with leading the annual feedback cycle. The same group that developed the plan should be evaluating its effectiveness. This ensures continuity and accountability.
Schedule an Annual Performance Technology Review Meeting (separate from regular Working Group meetings). This dedicated session should:
Review all feedback collected during the year (surveys, focus groups, incident reports).
Evaluate each technology against its stated purpose: is it delivering the expected value?
Identify any policy gaps, compliance issues, or areas where the plan needs updating.
Set priorities for the coming year (new trainings needed, technologies to add or remove, policy revisions).
Document decisions and updates in the plan revision log.
Produce an Annual Performance Technology Report (2-3 pages) summarizing findings and actions taken. Share with athletics administration.
Deliverable:
Annual Performance Technology Review Meeting Agenda Template and Annual Report Template. Target: First cycle completes Spring 2027.
Draft Template: Annual Review Meeting Agenda
Agenda Item | Led By | Time
1. Review of feedback: student-athlete survey results | Chair / Student-Athlete Reps | 20 min
2. Review of feedback: staff survey  results/observations | Chair | 15 min
3. Technology-by-technology effectiveness review | S&C / Sports Med | 20 min
4. Education program assessment:  Did  training meet needs? | Chair | 10 min
5. Policy compliance review: any incidents or gaps? | Legal / Compliance | 10 min
6. Proposed plan updates for  the  coming year | All | 15 min
7. Action items and next steps | Chair | 10 min
Strategy 5.2: Prioritize Student-Athlete Feedback
NCAA Strategy:  Understanding student-athletes' experiences with performance technology is critical. Schools should obtain student-athlete feedback to learn about the positive and/or negative impacts performance technology use has on their student-athletes.
Student-athlete feedback is the most important input in the continuous improvement process. The NCAA uses the word "critical" deliberately. We need a structured way to hear from student-athletes that goes beyond assuming they are fine because they have not complained.
Key Actions:
Develop an annual student-athlete survey. Administer once per year (recommended: end of spring semester) to capture the full year’s experience. Keep it short (10-15 questions) to maximize response rates.
Draft Template: Draft Student-Athlete Performance Technology Survey
# | Question | Response Type
1 | I understand what performance technology data is collected about me. | Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree (1-5)
2 | I understand who has access to my data and how it is used. | 1-5 scale
3 | I feel comfortable with how my data is being used. | 1-5 scale
4 | I was given adequate information before consenting to data collection. | 1-5 scale
5 | I feel that I can decline participation without negative consequences. | 1-5 scale
6 | The performance technologies used in my sport have helped my training or performance. | 1-5 scale
7 | I have experienced stress, anxiety, or negative feelings related to performance technology data (e.g., fixation on scores, body image concerns). | Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always
8 | If I had a concern about how my data was being used, I would know who to contact. | Yes / No / Unsure
9 | I have raised a concern about performance technology this year. | Yes / No
10 | If yes, my concern was addressed satisfactorily. | Yes / No / N/A
11 | The training I received about performance technology was helpful. | 1-5 scale
12 | Is there anything about how Baylor uses performance technology that you think could be improved? | Open text
13 | Is there anything about your experience with performance technology that concerns you? | Open text
Supplement surveys with qualitative feedback. Consider one or two annual focus group sessions with student-athletes from different sports. SAAC meetings can also serve as a forum for surfacing concerns. Qualitative feedback captures nuance that Likert scales miss.
Establish a confidential concern reporting channel. Student-athletes should have a way to raise concerns outside of surveys. This could be a dedicated email address, an anonymous online form, or a designated point of contact (e.g., the Data Steward or a member of the Student-Athlete Advisory Committee).
Share results with student-athletes. Close the feedback loop. Share a brief summary of survey findings and any actions taken at a SAAC meeting or through team communication. This builds trust and encourages future participation.
Deliverable:
Annual Student-Athlete Survey (digital, administered via survey platform). Confidential Concern Reporting Channel (email or anonymous form). Target: Survey launches Spring 2027; reporting channel established Fall 2026.
Strategy 5.3: Evaluate Implementation and Effectiveness
NCAA Strategy:  Areas for feedback from additional groups could  include:  technology implementation (e.g., how  were technologies  used),  technology  effectiveness (e.g., how did outcomes align with the school's reasons for their use), and education (e.g., does education meet  learner  needs).
Key Actions:
Develop a Staff Feedback Survey (brief, annual). Administer to all staff involved with performance technologies.
Draft Template: Draft Staff Performance Technology Survey
# | Question | Response Type
1 | The technologies I use are reliable and perform as expected. | 1-5 scale
2 | I have adequate training  to use  the technologies assigned to me. | 1-5 scale
3 | The data I receive from performance technologies is useful for my work. | 1-5 scale
4 | I understand the department's policies on performance technology use. | 1-5 scale
5 | I know who to contact if I have a data-related question or concern. | Yes / No
6 | Are there technologies you think we should add, change, or discontinue? Why? | Open text
7 | Is there additional training you would find helpful? | Open text
Conduct a technology-by-technology effectiveness review. For each technology in use, the Working Group should evaluate annually:
Implementation: Are we using it the way we intended? Are all staff following protocols?
Effectiveness: Are the outcomes matching the reasons we adopted it? Is it delivering measurable value?
Student-athlete impact: Is it causing any reported negative effects?
Cost: Is the ongoing cost justified by the value delivered?
Decision: Continue as-is / Modify usage / Discontinue.
Evaluate education effectiveness. Use training attendance records, survey feedback (both SA and staff), and observed knowledge gaps to determine whether education programs are landing. Update curriculum as needed.
Deliverable:
Annual Staff Survey, Technology Effectiveness Review Template, and Education Effectiveness Assessment. All part of the annual review cycle beginning Spring 2027.
Master Implementation Timeline
The following consolidates all five recommendations into a single timeline. The approach builds the foundation quickly, leverages existing structures, and targets full implementation by the start of the 2026-27 academic year, with the first complete feedback cycle closing in Spring 2027.
When | Key Deliverables | Rec. #
Mar 2026 | Form  Working Group, approve charter, conduct technology inventory, schedule legal meeting | 1, 3
Apr 2026 | Present  the  NCAA doc to S-A Staff, begin drafting written plan sections, start vendor contract audit | 1, 2, 3
May 2026 | Complete legal review of plan and consent form, finalize Data Access Matrix, build Tech Evaluation Checklist | 1, 3, 4
Jun 2026 | Finalize and approve  the  written plan, develop all education modules,  and  establish  a  confidential reporting channel | 1, 2
Jul 2026 | Distribute  plan  to all staff, begin updating consent forms for incoming student-athletes | 1, 2, 3
Aug 2026 | Deliver staff training at annual compliance meeting, SA training at orientation,  and  roll out updated consent process | 2, 3
Sep 2026 | Returning SA refresher during preseason, Working Group quarterly meeting, activate Tech Purchase Process | 2, 4
Fall 2026 | Full operation under new policies, collect informal feedback, document any incidents or issues | All
Jan 2027 | Mid-year Working Group check-in, address any urgent issues, new SA onboarding for spring admits | 1, 2
Spring 2027 | Administer SA and staff surveys, conduct technology effectiveness review, hold Annual Review Meeting, update plan | 5
Summary of Key Deliverables
Deliverable | Owner | Target Date
Working Group Charter | Chair (TBD) | March 2026
Technology Inventory | S&C + Sports Med | March 2026
Data Touchpoint Map | Working Group | April 2026
Data Access Matrix | Working Group + Legal | May 2026

Informed Consent Form Template | Legal | May 2026
Technology Evaluation Checklist | S&C + Sports Med | May 2026

Written Policy (full plan) | Working Group | June 2026
Education Modules (5 audiences) | Chair + Subject Leads | June 2026
Confidential Reporting Channel | Administration | June 2026
Annual SA Survey | Chair + Student-Athlete Reps | Spring 2027
Annual Staff Survey | Chair | Spring 2027

Closing
This plan is designed to be thorough but practical. We are leveraging existing structures wherever we can (annual compliance sessions, SAAC, campus IT, and legal), so this does not become an unsustainable burden on top of everything else the department is managing. The Working Group is the engine that keeps all of this moving, which is why standing it up first is the immediate priority.
This is a working document. It will get better with input from the people in the room. I am ready to start pulling the group together as soon as you give the green light.

BAYLOR ATHLETICS
Software and Technology Management Framework
Status | Draft for discussion
Date | August 14, 2026
Prepared by | Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Responsible offices | Intercollegiate Athletics; Information Technology Services; Office of General Counsel; University Compliance and Risk Services
Review and approval | Business Office and ITS serve as the two control points. Final policy language should be reviewed by the Office of General Counsel, University Compliance and Risk Services, ITS, and Privacy.
1. Purpose
To increase the efficiency and timeliness of requests for software and technology purchase and implementation, and to establish a consistent, transparent process for how those decisions are made, reviewed, and renewed.
1.1  Policy statement
Baylor Athletics shall select, acquire, implement, use, access, disclose, retain, and dispose of software, technology, and the data they generate only for authorized athletics, sports medicine, health, safety, performance, compliance, and operational purposes, and only in accordance with Baylor University policies, applicable law, NCAA guidance, contractual obligations, and approved data-governance practices.
Software and technology must be governed through a written plan, routine education, defined data rights, structured technology review, and continuous improvement.
1.2  Reason for the framework
Technology used in athletics may collect biometric, health-related, performance, workload, recovery, video, sensor, survey, software, mobile-application, and other individual-level data. Responsible use of these technologies requires coordination across Athletics, Sports Medicine, Information Technology Services, Privacy, Legal, Compliance, Procurement, and Records Management.
This framework is intended to help Baylor Athletics support student-athlete health, safety, privacy, autonomy, data security, and performance while reducing legal, regulatory, contractual, operational, and reputational risk.
The framework started with athlete performance technology, which handles the most sensitive data and is subject to the clearest NCAA guidance. It is written to serve as the department's general approach to all technology. The process below applies to every technology request in the department, and the depth of review depends on the request's scope.
2. Scope and terminology
2.1  Scope
Technology refers to tangible items like devices, wearables, equipment, and applications. Software refers to the platforms and systems those items connect to. The two are rarely purchased independently, and this framework covers both.
The framework is not limited to performance, health, and wellness. Athlete performance technology sits inside that scope and triggers a review. A request that does not involve any athlete data still goes through the same review mechanism.
2.2  Individuals and entities affected
Baylor Athletics staff, coaches, sports medicine personnel, strength and conditioning staff, analysts, administrators, student support staff, and other Baylor personnel who select, use, access, interpret, or disclose technology and the data it generates.
Student-athletes whose data is collected, used, analyzed, inferred, stored, or disclosed through these technologies.
Vendors, contractors, consultants, and other third parties that collect, store, process, analyze, host, transmit, or receive Baylor Athletics data on Baylor's behalf.
Baylor units supporting Athletics, including ITS, Information Security, Office of General Counsel, University Compliance and Risk Services, Privacy, Internal Audit, Procurement, and records-management functions.
2.3  Exclusions
This framework does not replace or supersede Baylor policies that already govern specific categories of data, systems, conduct, records, or legal obligations. Where a more specific Baylor policy applies, that policy continues to govern. This document should be read as an Athletics-specific overlay that routes technology decisions into existing Baylor governance channels rather than around them.
2.4  Definitions
Term | Definition for this framework
Technology | Tangible items such as devices, wearables, sensors, cameras, and equipment, together with the applications that operate them.
Software | The platforms and systems that technology connects to, including hosted, cloud, and on-premises applications.
Athlete Performance Technology | Any device, sensor, wearable, software, mobile application, camera, survey, analytics platform, AI-enabled system, or other technology used to collect, infer, monitor, analyze, store, or communicate biometric, performance, workload, recovery, wellness, health, safety, training, competition, or related data about student-athletes.
Athlete Performance Technology Data | Data collected, generated, inferred, stored, analyzed, or disclosed through athlete performance technologies, including performance metrics, physiological metrics, sleep, hydration, nutrition, stress indicators, recovery, training load, practice or game analytics, and related data.
Restricted / Protected Data | Data subject to Baylor data-classification requirements and heightened safeguards, including where applicable PHI, FERPA records, biometric identifiers, credentials, SSNs, financial information, IRB-related research data, and other regulated or sensitive data.
Medical Decision-Making Data | Data used, intended to be used, or reasonably likely to be used to inform medical management, injury evaluation, treatment, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions.
Approved Use Case | A documented and approved purpose, user population, data category, vendor or system, and data lifecycle for a technology.
Student-Athlete Notice | A plain-language explanation to student-athletes of what data is collected, why, who may access it, permissible uses, retention, rights, questions, and concerns.
3. Alignment with NCAA guidance
The NCAA Sports Science Institute has published guidance on the Responsible Use of Performance Technologies in College Athletics. That guidance sets the expectations each institution is to meet and leaves the method of implementation to the institution, according to its own structure and resources. This framework is Baylor Athletics' implementation. Appendix A maps each NCAA recommendation to the section of this framework that carries it.
4. Intended outcomes
A consistent, shared understanding of the entire inventory of software and technology in use across the department.
Improved utilization of what the department already owns.
Coordinated renewal and term review, giving the department advance visibility of contract end dates and the lead time to evaluate options well before a renewal decision is due.
Increased staff fluency so that sport administrators and unit staff can address technology questions with confidence.
5. Roles and responsibilities
The roles below combine the operating roles that move a request through the process with the review functions that must be applied before a request can clear.
Role | Responsibility in this framework
Head Coach, Admin, and/or Unit Director | Initiates the request. Completes the Idea Form and internal ATH Form, including the declared data category and proposed review level.
Athletics Executive Sponsor | Owns Athletics operational compliance with this framework and ensures teams, coaches, and staff use approved technologies and approved use cases.
Business Office | First control point.  Filters  all requests before they proceed. Budget, contract, and duplication check process through the Business Office.
ITS / Information Security | Second control point. Technical, security, and integration review; confirms the system can be supported. Reviews access, authentication, storage, transmission, monitoring, incident response, and security controls. These requests carry integration, contract, and security implications across departments, so ITS is represented at a supervisory level with the authority to commit ITS resources and to decide on integration and security posture. Technical staff are brought in for specialist review as the request requires.
Director of Applied Performance | Single point of contact and facilitator. Holds the weekly standing meeting with ITS and relays status to project managers and stakeholders. Facilitator, not owner; not the subject-matter expert and not the project manager.
Assigned Project Manager | Owns delivery of the individual project. May be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied Performance.
Sport Administrator | Signs off on renewal decisions at Phase 3, informed by the usage review.
Health & Wellness / Sports Medicine | Reviews requests involving physiologic or health data. Must be involved where data may inform medical decision-making, injury evaluation, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions.
Athletics Compliance | Coordinates NCAA, conference, student-athlete, and departmental compliance implications.
Office of General Counsel / Privacy | Reviews FERPA, HIPAA, Texas privacy, consent, data rights, disclosure, vendor terms, and legal holds.
Procurement / Contracting | Ensures vendor contracts address ownership, permitted use, storage, access, data sharing, AI training, automated decision-making, downstream sharing, retention, deletion, portability, and breach notification.
Coaches, Staff, and Users | Use technology only for approved purposes, complete required training, avoid unauthorized disclosure, and report suspected misuse or incidents.
Student-Athlete Representatives | Provide feedback on transparency, education, perceived benefits, and potential unintended impacts of technology use.
6. Levels of review
The level of review depends on three things: what data the technology touches, how many units it serves, and what the department is committing to in cost and contract term.
Level | Applies when | Review includes
Level 1 Standard Review | No athlete data; single unit; low or one-time cost | Compliance, Privacy, Ownership, Transparency, Interoperability
Level 2 Enhanced Review | Performance data, multi-team use, or recurring cost | Full review
Level 3 Comprehensive Review | Physiologic or health data; external data sharing; third-party processing of athlete data | Full review, plus data protection review and Health & Wellness / medical sign-off
The level is proposed by the requester at intake and confirmed at the control points.
7. Exceptions
7.1  Urgent and “emergency” requests
Urgent requests clear the same control points, with a short risk checklist completed at intake to surface issues that would otherwise delay the request: data category, contract term, integration dependency, and whether athlete data leaves Baylor.
A request directed by an administrative lead enters the expedited lane on receipt. This provides documentation for what qualifies as urgent, so the distinction does not have to be determined on a case-by-case basis at intake. An expedited request still clears both control points and still carries the review level its data and commitment call for.
8. The three phases
Phase 1 — Proposal, Approval, Purchase
1.1  A request is initiated by the Director of Applied Performance, a Head Coach, or any Admin Unit Director.
1.2  The requester completes the Technology Idea Form and the internal ATH Form. The request must declare its data category and proposed review level.
1.3  The request goes to the Business Office. The Business Office serves as the filter for all requests and the first control point.
1.4  The forms are submitted to ITS for technical, security, and integration review. This is the second control point. The Athletics steps described in this framework feed that review; they do not create a separate ITS workflow.
1.5  The request is evaluated against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard.
1.6  A request is disseminated for purchase only after clearing both control points. Declined requests are returned with documented reasons.
1.7  The Director of Applied Performance holds a weekly standing meeting with the ITS representative to review the status of all open requests across all units. The requester may be brought into the meeting where input is needed; their standing attendance is not expected. The Director of Applied Performance provides regular updates on the status of any open request.
Phase 2 — Implementation and Product Use
2.1  A project manager is assigned. This may be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied, depending on the unit and the system.
2.2  Status flows from the weekly ITS standing meeting through the Director of Applied to the assigned project manager and stakeholders, so that every open request has a known owner.
2.3  Open requests are tracked as follows: project, item, requester, project manager, date submitted, desired implementation date, current status, and what is holding it up.
Phase 3 — Product Review and Renewal Decision
3.1  Review is triggered at six months, or at the end of the competitive season, whichever is longer. Tools used primarily in season are therefore judged on in-season usage.
3.2  The review compares actual utilization against the intent stated on the original request.
3.3  Low utilization opens a diagnostic conversation before a renewal conclusion.
3.4  The outcome is renew, modify or renegotiate, or discontinue.
9. Workflow
Appendix A — NCAA Performance Technologies Recommendations Crosswalk
The NCAA Sport Science Institute's consensus guidance on the responsible use of performance technologies in college athletics is organized around five recommendations. The table below carries each recommendation, the NCAA strategy, the corresponding Baylor action step, and the section of this framework where it is addressed. Entries marked “planned for Version 1” identify work that is scoped and scheduled for the next revision of this document.
Recommendation | NCAA Strategy | Baylor Action Step | Framework Reference
1. Policy | Create a written plan. Build it with a multidisciplinary team (student-athletes, sports medicine, coaches, admin, legal, IT). Review it regularly. | Form a MDT (Multi-disciplinary Team) or a Performance Technology Working Group, draft the plan, and present it to S-A Services Staff for input. | §1.1  Policy statement — the written-plan requirement §1.2  Reason for the framework §5  Roles and responsibilities — review functions spanning sports medicine, compliance, legal, ITS, procurement, and Student-Athlete Representatives §8  Phase 1.7 — standing review cadence with ITS Standing Performance Technology Working Group and the framework’s own review cycle: planned for Version 1.
2. Education | Train everyone at least once a year. Tailor content by audience. Cover limitations, data privacy, informed consent, and departmental policies. | Add a performance technology module to existing compliance sessions and new student-athletes’ onboarding. Different content for coaches, Athletic Medicine, Athletics Performance, and student-athletes, etc. | §1.1  Policy statement — routine education as a governing requirement §5  Coaches, Staff, and Users — required training §5  Student-Athlete Representatives — feedback on education A dedicated Education and Training section, carrying annual cadence and audience-specific content: planned for Version 1.
3. Data Management | Establish who owns the data, where it lives, who can see it, and what it can be used for. Plan for transfer student-athletes. | Run a full technology inventory across all sports. Work with legal and IT to establish ownership, access, and transfer protocols. Develop a data rights/release consent template. | §1.1  Policy statement — authorized purposes; access, retention, and disposal §2.4  Definitions — Restricted / Protected Data; Medical Decision-Making Data; Approved Use Case; Student-Athlete Notice §4  Intended outcomes — department-wide technology inventory §5  ITS / Information Security — access, authentication, storage, transmission §5  Office of General Counsel / Privacy — consent, data rights, disclosure §5  Procurement / Contracting — ownership, permitted use, retention, deletion, portability §6  Level 3 Comprehensive Review — external data sharing; third-party processing Transfer student-athlete data protocol and the data rights / release consent template: planned for Version 1.
4. Tech Selection | Evaluate quality (accuracy, reliability, validity) before you buy. Use evidence-based frameworks. Decisions should be made by a cross-functional group. | Build a Technology Evaluation Checklist. Route all new purchases through the Working Group (MDT). Establish a scalable review process with documentation. | §5  Roles and responsibilities — cross-functional review functions §6  Levels of review — Level 1 Standard, Level 2 Enhanced, Level 3 Comprehensive §7  Exceptions — expedited requests clear the same control points §8  Phase 1.2–1.6 — Technology Idea Form and internal ATH Form; Business Office control point; ITS control point; Technology Evaluation Scorecard at 1.5; documented decision Quality criteria (accuracy, reliability, validity) are carried in the Technology Evaluation Scorecard, maintained as a companion artifact to this framework.
5. Continuous Improvement | Collect feedback from student-athletes, coaches, and staff on a regular basis. Student-athlete feedback is not optional. Use it to update the plan. | Annual student-athlete survey. The Working Group runs an annual review. Each technology gets a continuation, modification, or discontinuation decision. | §8  Phase 3.1–3.4 — review at six months or end of competitive season; utilization measured against stated intent; diagnostic conversation; outcome of renew, modify or renegotiate, or discontinue §5  Student-Athlete Representatives — feedback on transparency, education, perceived benefits, and potential unintended impacts Annual student-athlete survey and the annual Working Group review of the framework: planned for Version 1.
A.1  Foundational concepts
Two foundational concepts in the NCAA guidance sit alongside the five recommendations. The breadth of the NCAA definition of performance technology, which reaches cameras, surveys, and applications and not only wearables, is carried in the §2.1 scope statement and the §2.4 definition of Athlete Performance Technology. Student-athlete rights, informed consent, and the potential for unintended impacts, including effects on mental health and body image, are reflected in the §2.4 Student-Athlete Notice, the §5 Office of General Counsel / Privacy and Health & Wellness / Sports Medicine review functions, and the §5 Student-Athlete Representatives feedback role. Explicit treatment of unintended impacts within the education content and the annual student-athlete survey is planned for Version 1.
A.2  Relationship to institutional workflow
This framework is an Athletics-side overlay, as stated in §2.3. It routes technology decisions into the existing Baylor governance channels rather than around them. The Athletics intake and control points described in §8 are intended to complement institutional review rather than to operate as a separate workflow.=====
BAYLOR ATHLETICS  ·  APPLIED PERFORMANCE
Technology Evaluation Scorecard
Adapted from the Sports Tech Research Network Quality Framework for Sports Technologies, and from the existing Baylor Applied Performance assessment sheet.
Status | DRAFT v0.9 — for discussion, 2026-08-10
Completed by | Reviewer named below, at Phase 1
Applies to | Standard and Elevated tier requests in full; Light tier completes the gate features only
Product name | 
Vendor | 
Type of technology | 
Intended purpose | 
Context of use | 
Rater's name | 
Date | 
Review tier | Light / Standard / Elevated
How to use this scorecard
The scorecard has two parts that work differently.
Gate features are pass or fail. A fail on any gate feature stops the request regardless of how the rest of the scorecard reads. These are the features that create institutional risk or long-term lock-in, and they cannot be offset by strength elsewhere.
Scored features are rated Strong, Adequate or Weak. They inform the decision and the negotiation; they do not by themselves stop it. Use N/A where a feature genuinely does not apply, and say why in the note column.
Rating language follows the STRN convention: Strong — excellent, with no useful further improvement possible or only minor opportunity; Adequate — acceptable, with clear opportunities for improvement; Weak — a weakness needing improvement.
A fail is not necessarily the end A gate failure means the request cannot proceed as submitted. It is often the start of a conversation with the vendor — unclear data ownership terms and absent export capability are frequently negotiable, and asking for them is easiest before signature.
Part 1  ·  Gate features — pass / fail
Feature | Definition | Pass | Fail | Evidence / note
Compliance | The extent to which the technology is aligned with relevant laws and regulation. | ☐ | ☐ | 
Privacy | The extent to which the confidentiality of, and access to, information about the user is protected. | ☐ | ☐ | 
Ownership | The ability to access, create, modify, package, derive benefit from, sell or remove outputs, and to assign those privileges, is clearly defined. | ☐ | ☐ | 
Transparency | Recalls, feature updates, and honest, timely reporting to users and governing bodies. Security vulnerabilities are logged, disclosed and resolved. | ☐ | ☐ | 
Interoperability | Ability to connect to and communicate with other systems at foundational, structural or semantic levels. | ☐ | ☐ | 
Any fail above halts the request. Record the reason and, where relevant, what the vendor would need to change.
Part 2  ·  Evidence quality — does it measure what it claims?
Feature | Definition | Str | Adq | Wk | N/A | Evidence / note
Accuracy | Agreement of the technology's output with a current gold standard for similar measurement. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ | 
Repeatability | Output remains the same under similar test conditions over a short period. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ | 
Reproducibility | Output remains the same under changed conditions — different users, devices, locations, or extended time. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ | 
Specifications | Capacity, sample rate and dimensions are clearly available to the user. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ | 
Construct validity | Measures the specific area of interest, and differentiates between groups or conditions. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
